list.name: vLLM metrics unreachable
list.textFormat: Prometheus could not scrape vLLM here. Gaps are MISSING DATA, not idle time, and any gauge (KV, running, waiting) loses its peak.

panels.title: vLLM call p95 · budget ~2s
panels.description:
95th percentile of ONE vLLM call, over a 5-minute window (arrival to last token).

The platform SLO is p95 under 5s for a whole AGENT RUN, and one agent run is 2-3 dependent vLLM calls. So the per-call share of that budget is roughly 5 / 2.3 = 2s, and the colours encode both bounds:

  green  < 2s   per-call budget met, agent SLO comfortably reachable
  orange 2-5s   a single call is eating most of the agent's budget - 2-3 of these will miss 5s
  red    > 5s   one call alone already exceeds the whole agent budget

Orange is the interesting state: this panel can look survivable while the agent misses the SLO. Confirm end-to-end agent latency in Langfuse (Phase 4) or the load-test driver, not here.

Pinned to seconds rather than Grafana's auto-scaling time unit, so the number and the budget in the title share a unit and need no mental conversion - an overloaded server reads '234.1 s', not '3.90 mins'.

CAVEAT: this histogram's buckets step 2.5 -> 5.0 -> 10.0, so any p95 landing between 2.5s and 5s is linearly interpolated inside one very wide bucket, not observed. Use it for trend. For the SLO verdict use the panel to the right, which is exact.

panels.title: Calls under 5s
panels.description:
Share of individual vLLM calls that finished within 5 seconds, over a 5-minute window.

This reads the le="5.0" bucket counter directly, so it is an exact count, not an interpolated quantile - unlike any p95 on this dashboard.

Treat it as a FLOOR, not the SLO itself. The 5s SLO is on a full agent run of 2-3 dependent calls, so this being 100% does not prove the SLO held - but this being low proves it did not.

panels.title: Throughput
panels.description: Requests finishing per second, averaged over a 5-minute window, all outcomes. This is vLLM requests, not agent runs: one agent run is 2-3 of these, so divide by ~2.5 to compare against the 10 RPS agent-level SLO.

panels.title: Running / waiting
panels.description:
Requests currently in the batch vs queued for admission.

waiting > 0 sustained means the scheduler is turning work away - you are at the --max-num-seqs cap or out of KV blocks. Cross-check with the KV usage stat: if KV is low and waiting is high, the seq cap is the binding constraint.

panels.title: KV cache used
panels.description:
Fraction of the KV cache currently holding live sequence state. This is your concurrency headroom: at 100% the scheduler starts preempting.

Note the metric is a 0-1 fraction despite 'perc' in its name (vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc), hence the percentunit display.

panels.title: Preemptions (last 5 min)
panels.description:
Sequences evicted from the batch and restarted because KV ran out. Any non-zero value means you overcommitted concurrency and are now paying to recompute work you already did.

This should be zero. If it isn't, it explains a latency tail that nothing else on the dashboard accounts for.

panels.title: Latency - is it slow, and where?
End-to-end request latency
panels.description:
Full request latency as vLLM sees it: queue + prefill + decode. Dashed line is the 5s SLO.

p50 rising = everyone is slower (the system is saturated). p99 rising while p50 is flat = a tail problem - look at preemptions and queue depth, not at the average.

Bucket resolution above 2.5s is coarse (2.5 -> 5.0 -> 10.0), so treat values in that band as approximate.

panels.title: Where the time goes (mean, stacked to e2e)
panels.description:
THE 'where in the lifecycle' panel. Mean seconds per request per stage, stacked so the total equals mean e2e latency.

queue   -> waiting for a scheduler slot. Growing = admission-limited, you are at --max-num-seqs or out of KV.
prefill -> processing the prompt. Growing = longer prompts, or prefix caching stopped hitting.
decode  -> generating tokens. Growing = longer outputs, or a heavier batch.
unaccounted -> e2e minus the three above. See below - this is not a rounding error.

WHY 'unaccounted' EXISTS: vLLM starts the e2e timer when a request reaches the API server, but queue_time only starts when the ENGINE scheduler sees it. Time spent between the two - the front-end handoff, which backs up once requests pile up waiting - lands in e2e and in none of the stage metrics. Measured on this stack under overload: e2e 14.33s against queue 0.47 + prefill 0.05 + decode 1.44, so 86% of real latency was invisible until this band was added. Without it the panel stacks to ~2s while p95 reads 93s, and reads as healthy while the SLO burns.

A large unaccounted band means the bottleneck is upstream of the engine: the engine is keeping up, the front end is not. Shed load or raise concurrency; tuning decode will not touch it.

Deliberately means, not percentiles: percentiles do not add, so a stacked p95 chart would be a convincing lie. Means do. For the tail, use the p50/p95/p99 panel to the left.

panels.title: Time to first token
panels.description:
Prefill-side responsiveness: how long before the caller sees anything.

This histogram has fine buckets from 1ms up, so unlike e2e its quantiles are trustworthy.

Phase 1 finding: TTFT stayed nearly flat (71 -> 124ms) across a 7x load ramp. If TTFT starts climbing here, something changed - prefix cache misses or genuine prefill queueing.

panels.title: Inter-token latency
panels.description:
Decode-side cost: gap between successive output tokens. Multiply by output length to get most of the request's latency.

Phase 1 finding: this workload is decode-bound - ITL climbed 7.3 -> 19.4ms over the same ramp where TTFT stayed flat. So this panel, not TTFT, is where load shows up first.

Uses vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds, not the deprecated time_per_output_token_seconds.

panels.title: Token throughput
panels.description:
Tokens per second in (prompt, prefill work) and out (generation, decode work).

Prompt tokens counts what was submitted, including tokens served from the prefix cache - so this line staying high while GPU work stays low is prefix caching doing its job. Compare against the prefix cache hit rate panel.

panels.title: Requests finished / s, by outcome
panels.description:
Completion rate split by why the request ended.

stop   = model emitted a stop token. Normal.
length = output hit the token cap and was truncated mid-generation. For text-to-SQL that means a cut-off query, so this is a QUALITY alarm sitting in a throughput panel.
abort  = the client disconnected first, usually a timeout upstream.

Any sustained length/abort traffic invalidates eval numbers taken at the same time.

panels.title: Queue depth
panels.description:
Requests in the running batch vs waiting for admission.

running plateauing at a flat ceiling = you hit --max-num-seqs.
waiting climbing while running is flat = arrivals exceed what the scheduler will admit; queue time (see 'Where the time goes') is about to dominate latency.
Both low while latency is high = the problem is decode speed, not admission.

panels.title: Batch fullness (tokens per engine step)
panels.description:
How many tokens each forward pass actually processed, against the --max-num-batched-tokens budget of 4096 (dashed).

Sitting near the cap = prefill-bound, steps are full and requests are waiting their turn; raising the budget may help.
Sitting far below it = decode-bound, each step is one token per active sequence and the GPU is latency-limited, not throughput-limited. Phase 1 measured this workload in the second regime, which is why sweeping this flag changed nothing.

The dashed reference line is vector(4096), hardcoded to match --max-num-batched-tokens in scripts/start_vllm.sh. It is the one number on this dashboard that does not come from /metrics, so it needs editing by hand if that flag changes.

panels.title: Tokens per request
panels.description:
Prompt and output length distributions - the shape of the workload, not its volume.

Phase 1 concluded the largest remaining latency lever is output-token count, since latency is roughly ITL x output length. So a prompt change in Phase 3 that makes the model terser should show up here as p95 output falling, and in the e2e panel as latency falling with it.

Buckets are coarse 1-2-5 decades, so read these as magnitudes, not exact counts.

panels.title: KV cache utilization
panels.description:
Share of KV blocks holding live sequence state. This is the answer to 'can I run more concurrency?'.

Below ~50%: headroom, raise --max-num-seqs before anything else.
Approaching 100%: the scheduler will start preempting - check the panel to the right.

Phase 1 measured a 4.7% peak on the H100 config, so expect this to look almost flat. That is a real result, not a broken panel: KV is the most abundant resource here, which is why --kv-cache-dtype fp8 was rejected.

See the config table below for what 100% means in tokens.

Aggregated with max(): prometheus_client's multiprocess mode adds a pid label under --api-server-count > 1, exporting one slightly-stale copy per API server process. Those are copies of a single engine-wide value, not shards, so max() reads the freshest - never sum(), which would multiply usage by the API server count.

panels.title: Prefix cache hit rate
panels.description:
Fraction of prompt tokens served from cached KV instead of being recomputed. Measured in tokens, not requests.

Phase 1 measured 93.6% and showed prefix caching is worth roughly 2x on this workload - and that it pays out in inter-token latency, not TTFT, because uncached prefill chunks share engine steps with everyone else's decode.

A drop here is therefore a real regression: it means prompts stopped sharing a stable prefix (schema before question). Watch this panel whenever prompts change.

panels.title: Preemptions / s
panels.description:
Rate of sequences evicted from the batch because KV ran out, then restarted from scratch.

This is the eviction signal. Non-zero means you are past your concurrency headroom and burning GPU redoing work - it shows up as a latency tail that the mean panels will not explain.

Fix by lowering --max-num-seqs or raising --gpu-memory-utilization, not by chasing the latency tail directly.

panels.title: Cache configuration (what 100% actually means)
panels.description:
Static config the engine booted with, read from vllm:cache_config_info.

KV capacity in tokens = num_gpu_blocks x block_size. These arrive as Prometheus label STRINGS and PromQL cannot do arithmetic on a label string, so the utilization panel above can only be a percentage and this table supplies the denominator. Work it out by hand once per config.

Also confirms prefix caching is actually on - the hit-rate panel is meaningless if it is not.

CAVEAT: under --api-server-count > 1 this is exported by an API server process rather than the engine, and num_gpu_blocks reads None - the block count is known only to the engine. Take the real figure from the vLLM startup log ('GPU KV cache size: N tokens') when running multiple API servers.

The columns are chosen by sum by (...) in the query rather than by a field-filter transform. A transform that selects nothing renders as No data, which is indistinguishable from a dead metric; a query that selects nothing is visible in the query itself.

CAVEAT: num_gpu_blocks reads 'None' here. vLLM emits cache_config_info before memory profiling fills the block count in, so the multiplication above cannot be done from this table. The real value is in the vLLM startup log: 27716 blocks x 16 = 443,456 tokens of KV. Read the KV utilization panel as a percentage of that.

targets.expr: sum by (num_gpu_blocks, block_size, cache_dtype, enable_prefix_caching, gpu_memory_utilization, prefix_caching_hash_algo) (vllm:cache_config_info)
